Thing
THING
n. (rendering Hebrew dābār, Greek pragma and rēma)
From Old English thing, which meant an assembly or a matter brought before one — the Icelandic parliament is still the Althing. The English word therefore began as a word for a case under discussion and only later became the vaguest noun in the language. Hebrew dābār travels the same road in reverse: it means a word, and because a word spoken by God becomes an event, it also means a thing or matter. In Hebrew, word and deed are one noun.

Biblical Definition

Thing is the plainest word in the language, and Scripture uses it at the highest moments, where the question is what God is able to do. The pattern statement is put as a question to Abraham after Sarah laughs, and it is left hanging so that she must answer it: “Is any thing too hard for the LORD? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen 18:14). The same question is put back to God by Jeremiah, in a prayer, as a confession rather than an enquiry, and God repeats it to him: “Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me?” (Jer 32:27) — spoken while the Babylonians were besieging the city and the prophet had just been told to buy a field in it. Gabriel brings the same doctrine to Mary in its most compressed form: “For with God nothing shall be impossible” (Luk 1:37). Three impossibilities — a barren womb, a doomed nation, a virgin conception — and one answer given each time. The word also serves for the summing up of all human duty, where Ecclesiastes gathers a whole book of restless enquiry into a single sentence: “Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecc 12:13). And the Lord Jesus reduces the crowded life of Martha to the same simplicity — one thing is needful.

Webster 1828 Definition

Whatever exists or may be thought of; a matter, affair, or circumstance; and in Scripture the question is any thing too hard for the LORD, the one thing needful, and the whole matter of man's duty summed in fearing God and keeping His commandments.

THING, n. 1. An event or action; that which is done or which comes to pass; as, we hear of strange things.

2. Any substance; that which is created; any particular article or commodity.

3. A matter or affair under consideration; as, this thing shall not be done.

4. Used of persons in contempt or in pity; as, poor thing.

5. In Scripture, is any thing too hard for the LORD? Gen. 18. One thing is needful. Luke 10. The conclusion of the whole matter. Eccl. 12.

Key Scripture

Genesis 18:14 — "Is any thing too hard for the LORD? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son."

Jeremiah 32:27 — "Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me?"

Luke 1:37 — "For with God nothing shall be impossible."

Ecclesiastes 12:13 — "Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man."

Modern Corruption

The promise that nothing is impossible with God is detached from God's revealed purpose and turned into a warrant for whatever the believer wants, so that omnipotence is made to serve human ambition.

expand to see more

“Nothing shall be impossible” is among the most abused sentences in Scripture. Lifted out of Luk 1:37, it becomes a general guarantee that any desire held with sufficient faith must be granted, and it is preached in exactly that form wherever the prosperity teachers are heard. Its setting forbids the use. It is spoken by an angel to a young woman who has just been told something she did not ask for, would not have chosen, and which would cost her reputation and very nearly her betrothal — and her reply is not a claim but a submission: be it unto me according to thy word. The same is true of the other two occurrences. Sarah is told what God has appointed, not what she has requested; Jeremiah is told to buy a field in a city God has determined to give to Babylon. In every case the divine omnipotence is attached to a divine purpose, and the comfort of the doctrine lies precisely there: what God has promised, nothing can prevent.

The opposite corruption is practical rather than doctrinal, and it is the commoner sin among the orthodox: to confess that nothing is too hard for the LORD while praying and living as though a good many things were. Sarah laughed within herself, and the narrative does not treat this as a small thing — God asks why she laughed, and the question is not answered. Jeremiah, having confessed in prayer that there is nothing too hard for God, is immediately asked whether he believes it about the field he has just bought. The principle to recover is that this doctrine is meant to be applied to particulars: to a specific dead marriage, a specific hardened child, a specific besetting sin. Fear God, and keep his commandments (Ecc 12:13) is the whole duty; and the God so feared is the God for whom nothing is too hard.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dābār means both word and thing, since a word from God becomes an event; it is also the ordinary term for a matter or case. Greek pragma is a deed or matter, and rēma is a spoken word which, like the Hebrew, can mean the thing said.

expand to see more

Hebrew dābār (H1697) — word, matter, thing; the same noun for what is spoken and for what comes to pass, since God's word is His act.

Hebrew pālā' (H6381) — to be wonderful, extraordinary, too hard; the verb in is any thing too hard for the LORD (Gen 18:14).

Greek pragma (G4229) — a deed, matter, or thing done; the substance of things hoped for (Heb 11:1).

Greek rēma (G4487) — a spoken word, and by the Hebrew idiom the thing spoken of; the word behind nothing in Luk 1:37, literally no rēma shall be impossible.

Greek adunateō (G101) — to be without power, impossible; with God nothing shall be impossible (Luk 1:37).

Usage

"Of the question put to unbelief: is any thing too hard for the LORD? (Gen 18:14; Jer 32:27)."

"Of the annunciation: for with God nothing shall be impossible (Luk 1:37)."

"Of the summing up of duty: fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man (Ecc 12:13)."
